evidence.quote: The increased strength is mainly due to the transformation of the material microstructure from ferritic phase to martensite phase when the steel experienced temperatures above 800 °C, as explained by Huang and Young [31] for SS and by Ban et al. [35] for bimetallic steel.
At 1000 °C, the retention factor of Young’s modulus for CS was dropped significantly to as low as 0.54.
CS is able to retain its ultimate strength up to the nominal peak exposed temperature of 600 °C with a retention factor greater than 0.95.
the retention factor of ultimate strength for CS gradually decreases from around 0.95 at 600 °C to 0.76 at 1000 °C.
retention factors of LDSS at exposure temperature of 900 °C is 0.82 while it is 0.69 for CS.
retention factors of LDSS at exposure temperature of 900 °C is 0.82 while it is 0.69 for CS.
AA has the best retention of Young’s modulus (0.97 – 1.00) for nominal peak exposed temperature up to 500 °C.
the retention factor of Young’s modulus has dropped to 0.83 at the postfire temperature of 550 °C.
the 0.2% proof stresses of AA are substantially decreased, resulting the retention factor of 0.20 – 0.41 from 150 °C up to 550 °C.

AA (i.e., AA-6061 and AA-7075) is able to maintain its ultimate strength up to 150 °C, with retention factor around 0.98– 0.99, but will significantly decrease to the range of 0.48 – 0.56 when the nominal peak exposed temperature over 150 °C.
the retention factors of ultimate strain for AA-6061 can reach 2.4 as heated up to 550 °C.
This phenomenon can be explained by the formation of martensite in the ferritic structure.
Such rebound of 0.2% proof stress could be explained by reappearance of second-phase particles and grain boundaries of AA as the temperature increases.

evidence.quote: The increased strength is mainly due to the transformation of the material microstructure from ferritic phase to martensite phase when the steel experienced temperatures above 800 °C, as explained by Huang and Young [31] for SS and by Ban et al. [35] for bimetallic steel.

For ferritic SS, after the decrease, it is found that the 0.2% proof stress will increase again as it is heated up to 750 – 900 °C. This phenomenon can be explained by the formation of martensite in the ferritic structure.

Some of the studies suggested that the postfire 0.2% proof stress of AAs will be increased again after certain temperature (e.g., at 450 °C for AAs 6061-T6). Such rebound of 0.2% proof stress could be explained by reappearance of second-phase particles and grain boundaries of AA as the temperature increases.
